title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: France seeks EU sanctions on Iran over refrigeration sabotage as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks on industrial controls
items.content_text: France asked EU partners on 16 November to sanction those it blames for October’s sabotage of refrigeration at about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and expects a decision on 14 December. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned the same day that tampering with cold-storage controllers threatens donor blood and therapies, not just data, after settings were changed at French blood-service sites. The campaign is wider than refrigeration: US and Israeli officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers have sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. Unpatched Danfoss AK-SM 800A flaws and newly probed Copeland XWEB EVO flaws keep the door open. Treat any internet-reachable controller as a proven target.

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and also reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. On 10 November Sweden warned that more incidents are likely after refrigeration was tampered with at seven Coop stores and an undisclosed number of ICA stores on 2 November; its NCSC says the victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer protected by weak passwords. On 12 November Belgium’s interior minister said evidence on the Belgian attacks points to Iran but stopped short of an official attribution (see top story); a pro-Russian claim is unverified, and France has formally attributed only the separate 12 October attack, to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Exposure is falling but not gone: exposed Danfoss StoreView instances dropped from 3,004 to 708 between 9 October and 5 November (The Hacker News, 9 November). Sekoia reported on 10 November that the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account, apparently a step towards resetting its password, and assesses that both waves may come from the same actor. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today.

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, about a week after fixes shipped, then used a local flaw in the gateway’s DynamicCLI service (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted web shells and backdoors named TSGA and TSProxy, scanned the internal network, moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper that overwrites and deletes files. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached gateways in several countries and sectors with no destruction seen. The backdoors resemble tooling linked to the China-nexus group UNC5221, but Check Point does not attribute the campaign with confidence. CISA added CVE-2026-123039 to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi hosts often run HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified on 29 October that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to gain root on about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October, then stole Active Directory credentials. Victims were in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea. The OT exposure widened: Siemens now lists Spectrum Power grid-control systems and AMIS TS, Schneider lists a Foxboro DCS server, and ABB lists Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways, several with no fix yet. Attribution is suspected, not confirmed, and no Siemens, Schneider or ABB product is reported exploited. No OT operator has been named, so treat this as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: A malicious update to drone ground-control software disrupted operations at German defence supplier Quantum Systems, reports say
items.content_text: Quantum Systems, a German maker of military reconnaissance drones, says it detected an incident in late October that was part of an active attack by “hostile actors,” and that it worked with authorities so its unmanned systems could safely resume operations. Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, report that the attackers pushed a malicious update to QBase, the company’s ground-control and mission-planning software, from the vendor’s own update server; it is unclear how many customers installed it. The German armed forces reportedly grounded the company’s drones as a precaution and left them out of a recent exercise. The company believes it was targeted for supporting Ukraine but names no attacker. For OT owners the lesson is wider than defence: a vendor’s update channel for control or engineering software is a direct path onto operational systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: Maersk confirms data was taken from an inherited legacy system as WhiteArmor demands $5 million; shipping operations unaffected
items.content_text: Maersk said on 11 November that attackers accessed a local legacy IT system it inherited through an earlier acquisition and extracted data. Its preliminary findings point away from sensitive data being exposed, and it sees no sign of impact on other Maersk systems or on customer and partner connections over APIs and EDI; customers can keep booking and managing shipments. The WhiteArmor extortion group claims about 100GB, including driver records, administrator accounts and delivery receipts, and wants $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. It ties the data to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought in 2022, but Maersk has not named the system. The lesson for OT owners is acquisition hygiene: inherited networks and accounts are often the least-watched path into a parent company (editorial assessment).

items.title: Volt Typhoon has used a rotating “Silent Train” relay network since 2023 to break into management platforms, with water, energy and transport among the victims, Lumen reports
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October that Volt Typhoon has used “Silent Train”, a covert network of rapidly rotating, single-use chains of compromised small-office routers, IoT and enterprise devices, since November 2023 to reach targets and keep access to management and control-plane systems. Lumen ties the group to four confirmed zero-day campaigns and one likely one: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0, Cisco), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876), Versa Director (no CVE given) and, with moderate confidence, Quest KACE (no CVE). These are older flaws, not the VeloCloud flaw CVE-2026-114625 that CISA added to KEV on 23 October. Victims include telecoms, government, defence contractors, IT firms and MSPs, and universities, and Lumen lists water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation and emergency services among the critical-infrastructure sectors hit; Hawaii, California and Texas recur as focal points (Zero Day). No victim is named and no OT or ICS intrusion is described. Lumen points defenders to CISA’s Volt Typhoon guidance (AA24-038A) and its advisory on China-nexus covert networks (AA26-113A). Management and orchestration platforms often hold trusted paths into plant networks, which makes them the asset to protect here (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hijacked Copeland XWEB refrigeration controllers are relaying spam and proxy traffic, and one intrusion pushed setpoints to 150 °C
items.content_text: SecurityScorecard’s STRIKE team reported on 9 November that internet-exposed Copeland XWEB PRO controllers, which run supermarket freezer and chiller racks, are being abused as spam relays and proxy exits; one unit in Trinidad and Tobago contacted more than 10,000 hosts in 17 hours. It suspects CVE-2026-25085, a login-bypass flaw among the 23 that Claroty Team82 reported and CISA published in February (ICSA-26-057-10), but has not confirmed the entry route. Separately, Ransom-ISAC analysed a 2 November intrusion in which attackers simply used the factory default administrator login, read settings on 31 devices and made 743 changes, including setpoints of 110 and 150 °C, muted alarms and locked keypads. Neither team links its findings to the Iran-attributed European attacks, but a second refrigeration platform is now being actively abused (editorial assessment).

items.title: SANS survey: OT incidents up 1.7× in a year, and leaders are far more confident than engineers that plants can run without IT
items.content_text: The SANS 2026 ICS/OT survey found that 34% of respondents had an industrial cyber incident in the past year, 1.7 times the 2025 rate and the biggest one-year rise SANS has recorded, and 72% of those incidents caused downtime. Fewer were caught quickly: 41% were detected within 24 hours, down from more than half in the two previous years. The sharpest gap is in resilience. Every security leader surveyed expected their plants to keep running through a full IT compromise, yet only 15% of practitioners said critical processes could run safely by hand for more than 48 hours, and 40% did not know. Only 16% have fully folded OT into business-continuity planning, and 68% said losing one or two veteran staff would slow response or create serious operational risk. Dedicated OT detection platforms caught more incidents (38%) than any other method, but budget remains the main barrier to wider deployment. For defenders, the practical point is to test the manual-operation assumption before an attacker does (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hacktivist-espionage group used Log4Shell in an unpatched vCenter to reach a software maker’s code-signing server, Kaspersky ICS CERT says
items.content_text: Kaspersky ICS CERT has described a months-long intrusion at an unnamed Russian software developer by BO Team (also tracked as Black Owl), a group it assesses as Ukrainian-origin and focused on espionage and hacktivism. The attackers came in through an exposed SSH service on a Linux terminal server, used the four-year-old Log4Shell flaw to take root on a VMware vCenter 7.0.3 server, then dumped credentials and moved through the domain controller, Ansible and GitLab. Their clear interest was the Windows server that signs the company’s commercial software builds, which points to either poisoning releases before signing or stealing the signing certificate. They were cut off before reaching it, and no malicious release is confirmed. The lesson travels: vendors that ship engineering and control software are targets because their signed updates are trusted on plant systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: An exposed server shows an espionage group running a DeepSeek-powered AI agent inside Tajikistan’s railway network, CloudSEK says
items.content_text: CloudSEK reported on 11 November that a misconfigured server linked to the Silent Lynx espionage cluster exposed months of operator logs. From mid-August to at least 10 October the group held administrator access in Tajikistan’s railway IT network: it dumped domain credentials including krbtgt, copied dispatcher summaries and operational reports from file shares, harvested credentials for upstream ISP network gear and planted a web shell, then used a railway account to reach a government document platform. Much of the work ran through an open-source autonomous agent using DeepSeek and Gemini models, with destructive commands pre-approved and Russian-language tasking over Telegram; the agent even tried to clean up its own logs. CloudSEK assesses a Kazakhstan nexus at medium confidence. No signalling or control system was touched, but the case shows AI agents carrying out whole intrusions inside a transport operator (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hackers probe 14 newly disclosed flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers, five of which will never be fixed
items.content_text: VulnCheck has disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO, the Dixell supervisory system that runs supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, each of which gave its researcher root on test units. Nine affect only firmware built before a 2021 rewrite and include unauthenticated command execution and a hard-coded admin password. The other five reach the latest firmware: the daily admin password is derived from the device’s MAC address and the date, and the MAC address is visible without logging in, so an attacker can compute the password, turn on SSH and log in as root. VulnCheck’s sensors saw exploitation attempts against two older-firmware flaws within two hours of the 12 November CVE publication; it calls the sources opportunistic scanners, not the state campaign in France. Copeland ended XWEB EVO support on 16 March 2026 and will not fix the five current-firmware flaws; nearly 2,000 units are reachable from the internet.

items.title: Six unpatched pre-login flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers prompt Belgian, German and Irish warnings to pull them off the internet
items.content_text: Amsterdam consultancy Midnight Blue has disclosed six stack buffer overflows in Danfoss AK-SM 800A system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, that allow remote code execution without logging in; one works even with “strict” session control turned on. All firmware up to 5.3.2 is affected and CVEs are still pending. The BSI says the 5.4.0 package released this month is not affected, but Midnight Blue says 5.4.0 predates its research and does not fix these bugs, so treat 5.4.0 as unconfirmed until Danfoss says otherwise. The researchers say an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset or firmware update, or brick units, because the device does not appear to use secure boot; that is a stated possibility, not a demonstrated one. Belgium’s CCB and Germany’s BSI (13 November) and Ireland’s NCSC have all told operators that firmware updates, password changes and strict mode are not enough for internet-exposed units. Danfoss had published no advisory or fix date as of 16 November. No exploitation of these six flaws is reported.

items.title: ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens finds the exploited Node2Shell bug in SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, and more OT vendors confirm PHP2Shell exposure
items.content_text: Siemens published nine advisories on 11 November covering ten flaws, two of them describing how the exploited Node2Shell (Brotli) bug reaches its products. High-severity issues touch SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, SIMATIC WinCC Graphics Designer, meta-iot2050, ROS#, Simcenter Femap and the Mendix Studio Pro MCP server, and could allow code injection or system compromise. Several products have no fix yet and some versions will not be fixed, so Siemens points customers to mitigations; it has seen Node2Shell exploitation attempts but no attacks aimed at its products. Schneider Electric fixed a medium-severity file-handling flaw in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, Johnson Controls fixed EasyIO Neo IO Manager and a C•CURE 9000/victor installer that could expose admin credentials, and Hitachi Energy and Phoenix Contact confirmed PHP2Shell impact. A day earlier CERT@VDE flagged a dozen bugs in Helmholz’s myREX24V2 remote-access server (fix 2.21.0) and two PHP2Shell use-after-free flaws in MB connect line’s mbCONNECT24/mymbCONNECT24 remote-maintenance portal that allow unauthenticated code execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVSS 3.1 9.8; CVE-2026-109619, 8.1; fixed in 2.21.6), and Axis rated a Camera Station flaw 9.9 (CVE-2026-13312).

items.title: N-central exploits now reach patched servers: attackers planted miners on 21 servers, 19 of them already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: On 9 November a researcher published “Able2Shell”, 33 flaws in N-able’s N-central remote monitoring and management platform with proof-of-concept code, and N-able shipped N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 the next day. The same researcher, Sean Bales, has since disclosed two new chains, 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, that he says work against the latest version; one uses a critical Apache Axis flaw, CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS 9.8). On 13 November Huntback reported cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, mostly in the US, South Africa, Canada, the UK, Germany, France and Sweden, and Previdian described the attack path. N-able is restricting features, has turned off the Legacy API and Intune integration on hosted servers, and tells customers to upgrade Agents and Probes to 2026.4 HF1 or later and disable the Legacy API on premises, with more fixes coming. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers are pushing rogue ScreenConnect clients through hijacked remote-support panels, reaching 288 endpoints at 48 organizations
items.content_text: Huntress reported on 12 November that, from the evening of 11 November, attackers used the Run Command feature in cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients and a toolkit it calls SCKit on at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organizations. The malware steals technicians’ session cookies, so a technician who connects to an infected machine can hand the attacker access to other customer sessions, letting it spread from client to client. Huntress suspects stolen credentials or hijacked sessions, and ConnectWise says it has found no compromise of its own infrastructure. Separately, Blackpoint Cyber said on 12 November that SCKit exploits CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9), a ScreenConnect flaw patched and added to CISA KEV in September, and that a fully patched client blocks its payload. No industrial victim is named, but many integrators and service providers support plant systems through ScreenConnect, so a compromised technician is a direct path into OT (editorial assessment).

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor.

items.title: CISA launches an Installed Base Program to work with OT manufacturers on finding and securing their internet-exposed equipment
items.content_text: On 10 November CISA announced the Installed Base Program, a voluntary partnership with original equipment manufacturers to identify internet-exposed OT devices across critical infrastructure and get them secured. The approach pairs what CISA sees on the internet with what manufacturers know about where their products are installed, so that owners can be warned sooner. Where it cannot tell who owns an exposed device, CISA says it may use administrative subpoenas to identify the owner. The launch follows weeks in which exposed refrigeration controllers were sabotaged at scale (see Incidents & Attacks). Operators should expect more direct notices, from CISA or their vendors, about equipment they may not know is reachable.
